# What Makes an Estimator Good

## An Estimator Is a Rule, Fixed Before the Draw

This section asks what makes one estimating rule better than another. We want
average hourly earnings in the population and we hold 120 people:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\bar{y} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i
\end{equation}
```

::: {.defn title="A Rule Before, a Number After"}
An estimator turns a sample into a number, by a rule fixed beforehand. An
estimate is the number one sample gives.
:::

::: {.notes}
IDEA 1, 10-32 min. The rule is fixed in advance and does not depend on which
120 people turn up. Put on the board: the same formula, two different samples,
two different numbers. That is the distinction the whole lecture needs, and it
is the one students skip.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2a, p.715: an estimator is a rule assigning each possible
     sample outcome a value; the rule is specified before any sampling is
     carried out. Estimate = the realised number. Equation is C.1, p.715.
     Notation list dropped: y_i and n were introduced in Lecture 1.1. -->
```

## A Hat Marks the Sample Counterpart

Every quantity in this lecture has two versions, one unknowable and one computed:

- $\mu$: average hourly earnings over the whole population
- $\bar{y}$, also written $\hat{\mu}$: the same quantity from our 120

::: {.defn title="The Hat Marks the Sample"}
A bare Greek letter is a population quantity, fixed and unknown. The hat marks
its sample counterpart: a rule before the draw, a number after it. So $\mu$
never changes, and $\bar{y}$ changes with every sample.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, and slowly. A student who reads mu-hat and mu as one object cannot
be taught sampling variation, and every later confusion in this deck traces
back here. The bar on y is convention for the mean only; from Lecture 2.1 the hat
is the general form.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-7, p.743: theta-hat denotes BOTH an estimator and an
     estimate. C-2a, p.715, is where the two are separated. CORRECTION: the
     previous version defined the hat as "a number we computed from a
     sample", which drops the estimator half and contradicts the rest of the
     deck. Fixed to name both. -->
```

## Four Candidate Estimators of the Population Mean

Each rule below could be written down before any data arrive:

- **Rule A:** Average all 120.
- **Rule B:** Average the first ten drawn, discard the rest.
- **Rule C:** Report 12.00 euro, whatever the sample says.
- **Rule D:** Drop the top and bottom five per cent, average the rest.

::: {.takeaway title="Rule C Is an Estimator"}
Rule C meets the definition: a rule, fixed in advance, returning a number.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Rule C is not a joke. It is legal, it is cheap, and it has one
property rule A does not have, which the next two frames name. Rule B is
Wooldridge's own counter-example enlarged from one observation to ten.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2b, p.718, uses W = Y_1, the first observation only, as the
     unbiased-but-poor estimator. Rule B is that example with ten draws
     instead of one. C-2d, p.720, uses the constant-zero rule as the biased
     zero-variance estimator; rule C is that rule at 12.00. -->
```

## Unbiased, Consistent and Efficient

Two rules can both be right on average, and one still lands closer. Three
properties, asked separately, say which rule to prefer:

- **Unbiased:** Over the samples we might have drawn, the rule returns $\mu$.
- **Consistent:** As $n$ grows without bound, the rule concentrates on $\mu$.
- **Efficient:** Of two unbiased rules, the one with smaller sampling variance.

::: {.caveat title="Only in the Linear Unbiased Class"}
The sample mean is least variable only among linear unbiased rules. The result
also needs a common mean, a common variance and uncorrelated draws.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, and the separation is the point. Unbiasedness is a finite-sample
property: it holds at n = 10 exactly as it holds at n = 10,000. Consistency is
about a sequence of sample sizes. Efficiency is only defined by comparison, and
only between rules that are already unbiased.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2b, p.716, equation C.3: E(W) = theta for all theta.
     C-3a, p.721, equation C.7: P(|W_n - theta| > e) -> 0. C-2d, p.719:
     relative efficiency is defined between TWO UNBIASED estimators.
     C-2d, p.720: "If we do not restrict our attention to unbiased
     estimators, then comparing variances is meaningless."
     C-2d, p.720, Problem C.2, for the linear-unbiased-class caveat.
     EXPOSITION PASS: the three properties moved out of the .defn into
     bullets, wording unchanged, so the linear-class restriction could take
     the frame's one callout. The body line on unbiasedness holding at any n
     went to the notes, where it already appeared. -->
```

## How the Four Rules Score

No rule wins on every count, and the steadiest one is always wrong:

- **Rule A:** Unbiased, consistent, and least variable among linear unbiased rules.
- **Rule B:** Unbiased at every $n$, and inconsistent: ten people stay ten people.
- **Rule C:** Never varies, and is wrong by 0.48 euro every time.
- **Rule D:** Less variable than rule A, and biased downwards by the tail.

::: {.takeaway title="Bias and Variance Are Traded"}
Mean squared error is the average squared distance from $\mu$. It equals
variance plus bias squared, and that sum ranks rule D against rule A.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Rule A's variance is sigma-squared over n, rule B's is
sigma-squared over ten, and the second does not fall as the sample grows. Rule
C's bias is 12.00 minus 11.52, which is 0.48. Rule D buys stability with a
little bias, and whether that is a good bargain depends on what the number is
for. The appendix derivations cover rule A's first two properties.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTION 1. Rule A was previously said to be "all three", with
     efficiency defined as smallest variance among ALL unbiased rules.
     Wooldridge C-2d, p.720: the sample average has the smallest variance
     among unbiased estimators that are also LINEAR functions of the data,
     under common mean, common variance and pairwise uncorrelated draws
     (Problem C.2). "Linear" added here and in the defn on the previous
     frame.
     CORRECTION 2. Rule C's bias read 0.80. 12.00 - 11.52 = 0.48.
     MSE = Var + Bias^2 is C-2d, p.720.
     NOT ON THE SHELF: rule D sitting below mu under a right tail is a
     property of this module's simulated population, not a Wooldridge
     result. Confirm against the generator. -->
```

## Why Unbiasedness Alone Is Not Enough

Unbiasedness makes two claims, and the second is weaker than students expect:

- **Across Samples:** The rule returns $\mu$ on average over repeated draws.
- **In One Sample:** Nothing, not even that 12.25 is anywhere near $\mu$.

::: {.caveat title="Unbiased and Still Worthless"}
Rule B is unbiased. Ten people give an answer close to worthless, so sampling
variance comes next.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Wooldridge's sentence is that unbiasedness does not mean the
estimate from any particular sample is equal to the parameter, or even close to
it. Say it twice. This is the sentence that stops a student reading 12.25 as
"the unbiased answer" and therefore the right one.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2b, p.717: "Unbiasedness does not mean that the estimate we
     get with any particular sample is equal to theta, or even very close to
     theta." C-2c, p.718: unbiased estimators exist that are quite poor. -->
```

## Choosing Among Three Imperfect Rules

You want average hourly earnings for Irish workers, and rule A is unavailable.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Rule B, rule C or rule D: which would you defend, and on what ground?
:::


::: {.notes}
32-35 min. "You may not pick A" is what makes this a question. Most rooms go to
D, which is the interesting answer, because it means they have accepted bias in
exchange for stability without being told that was allowed. Take answers out
loud and do not adjudicate. If there is time: one sentence each on what it
would mean for an estimator to be unbiased and useless.
:::

# The Sampling Distribution

## What One Estimate Leaves Open

This section describes how our estimate varies across different samples of 120.
Our sample gave 12.25, and that one number cannot separate draw from population:

- **What Varies:** The estimate, from one sample of 120 to the next.
- **What Does Not:** The population mean $\mu$, which is one fixed number.

::: {.defn title="The Estimate Has Its Own Distribution"}
$\bar{y}$ varies across samples, and that variation has a distribution: the
sampling distribution. Every property in this lecture belongs to it.
:::

::: {.notes}
IDEA 2, 35-65 min, and this is the frame to go slowly on. Wooldridge's phrase
is that the distribution of an estimator describes the likelihood of various
outcomes across different random samples. Angrist and Pischke put the same
point as: drawing another sample, we would get somewhat different results.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2b, p.716: "The distribution of an estimator is often called
     its sampling distribution, because this distribution describes the
     likelihood of various outcomes of W across different random samples."
     MM appendix to ch.1, p.33, for the framing. -->
```

## Five Hundred Samples, Five Hundred Means

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Means of 500 samples of 120; truth 11.52, our sample 12.25.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Our 12.25 Is One Draw"}
Our 12.25 is one draw from that histogram. A different 120 people lands
somewhere else in it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes at the picture. Walk it: each bar is one sample of 120, each
sample gave one mean, and the histogram collects five hundred of them. Green is
the truth at 11.52. The dashed navy line is our one sample at 12.25, which sits
to the right of the truth by chance and not by any fault of the rule. Ask where
they would have to stand to see this picture in real work; the answer is
nowhere.
:::


## The Sampling Distribution Is Not Observable

In real work you draw once, compute once, and never see that histogram:

- **What We Have:** One sample, one number, and a standard error.
- **In This Module:** We wrote the population, so we can draw repeatedly.

::: {.caveat title="Simulation Shows What Data Cannot"}
No dataset gives the sampling distribution. Simulation shows it here, and
theory stands in for it everywhere else.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. This is the entire reason the module has a simulated population.
From Lecture 2.1 the histogram is gone and the standard error is all that is
left, so the histogram is what they should picture whenever they read one.
:::

## Spread Across People and Spread Across Samples

Two numbers describe our sample, and they measure different things:

- **5.91:** How far one person's earnings sit from another's.
- **0.54:** The typical distance between our answer and the next sample's.

::: {.caveat title="Spread Across Samples Is Smaller"}
Dividing by $\sqrt{n}$ converts spread across people into spread across
samples. Confusing the two is this section's commonest error.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Earnings in the sample run from almost nothing to over
thirty-five euro, and the five hundred sample means all sit between about ten
and thirteen. Same population, two completely different pictures. Angrist and
Pischke make the same warning: do not confuse standard errors with the standard
deviations of the underlying variables.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-5c, p.733: sigma measures spread in the distribution of Y;
     sigma/sqrt(n) is the sampling standard deviation of Y-bar. MM appendix
     to ch.1, p.37, on the same confusion. -->
```

## The Standard Error of the Sample Mean

Errors partly cancel in a sum, so averages vary less than people do. Our 120
people are all we have to measure the spread across samples:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{se}(\bar{y}) \;=\; \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\end{equation}
```

- $s$: the standard deviation of the 120 earnings we drew
- $\mathrm{se}(\bar{y})$: the estimated standard deviation of $\bar{y}$

::: {.takeaway title="Variances Add, Spreads Do Not"}
Variances add and standard deviations do not, hence the root. Here
$5.91/\sqrt{120} = 0.54$, so four times the data halves it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Say the cancelling out loud: one person far above the mean is
usually offset by someone below, and the more people you add the more of that
offsetting there is, which is why root n and not n sits under the s. Then two
steps, and they are separate. First, the sampling variance of the mean is
sigma-squared over n, which needs independent draws with a common variance;
that is what random sampling buys. Second, sigma is unknown, so s goes in its
place and the result is called a standard error rather than a standard
deviation. The appendix derives the formula in three lines and does the first
step. Do not give the fourfold number away here; the next frame asks for it.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2c, p.718, equation C.6: Var(Y-bar) = sigma^2/n, using
     independence of the Y_i. C-5b, p.730: se(y-bar) = s/sqrt(n), the point
     estimate of sd(Y-bar). ARITHMETIC CHECKED: 5.91/sqrt(120) = 0.5395. -->
```

## How the Standard Error Falls With Sample Size

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Means of 500 samples at n = 30, 120 and 480, on one shared axis.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Four Times the Data Halves the Spread"}
The square root sets the rate. Four times the data halves the spread, and
sixteen times halves it again.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Walk the three panels left to right: same population, same truth,
same five hundred repetitions, only n changes. All three are centred in the
same place, which is unbiasedness, and only the width changes, which is the
standard error. Ask what n would be needed to halve 0.54; the answer is 480.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- FIGURE 1-3_samplesize: three histograms of 500 sample means at n = 30,
     120, 480, on a SHARED horizontal axis or the comparison is lost. Truth
     marked on each. -->
```

## The Central Limit Theorem, and What It Requires

Averaging washes out the shape of whatever population you started from. An
extreme average needs many people extreme the same way, which is rare.
Bell-shaped averages are what let one estimate carry a margin of error:

- **The Standardised Mean:** Subtract $\mu$ from $\bar{y}$, then divide by $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
- **The Large-Sample Shape:** A standardised mean is approximately standard normal.

::: {.caveat title="Large Samples, Finite Variance"}
The theorem needs random sampling and a finite population variance, and it
improves as $n$ grows.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Three things make the statement, and dropping any one of them
makes it false: random sampling, a finite population variance, and a large n.
Note also what is standardised - the theorem is about the standardised mean,
not about the mean itself, and the multiplication by root n is what keeps the
variance from collapsing to a point. Wooldridge says large-sample
approximations have been known to work well from about n = 20; Angrist and
Pischke's figures show the t-statistic already close to normal at n = 100.
In practice we treat y-bar as approximately normal with mean mu and variance
sigma-squared over n, which is the same statement rearranged.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTION 3. The old frame was headed "Why Sample Means Are Normal" and

     close-to-normal average. Wooldridge C-3b, p.724, equation C.12: for a
     random sample with mean mu and variance sigma^2, Z_n = sqrt(n)(Y-bar -
     mu)/sigma has an ASYMPTOTIC standard normal distribution. The finite
```

## A Skewed Population and a Symmetric Average

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Left: earnings in the population. Right: means of 500 samples of 120.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Population Stays Skewed"}
The population keeps its long right tail. Only the distribution of the average
has gone close to symmetric.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The point only lands if the left panel is obviously not normal, so
name the tail before moving right. Then say what changed between the panels:
not the population, only what is being plotted. Angrist and Pischke run the
same demonstration with a dummy variable that takes two values, where the
underlying distribution is two spikes and the t-statistic is still bell-shaped.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- FIGURE 1-3_clt: two panels. Left, the population density of earnings,
     visibly right-skewed. Right, the sampling distribution of the mean at
     n = 120 with a normal curve overlaid. The point only lands if the left
     panel is obviously not normal.
     MM appendix to ch.1, figures 1.2-1.4, pp.40-42: t-statistic at n = 10,
     40 and 100 for a Bernoulli(0.8) variable. -->
```

## What the Central Limit Theorem Does Not Say

The theorem is about averages, and says nothing about the people behind them:

- **Not About One Person:** Earnings stay skewed, and poor workers outnumber rich ones.
- **Not Exact:** Normality improves with $n$ and never holds exactly at 120.
- **Two Conditions:** Random sampling, and a population variance that is finite.

::: {.caveat title="Finite Samples Get No Guarantee"}
Nothing here says $\bar{y}$ is normal in our 120. The theorem describes a
limit, and 120 buys a good approximation to it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes, and this is the frame that pays for itself in Lecture 2.3. The
theorem arrives without our asking: we never assumed earnings were normal, and
they are not. What it gives is one formula that serves every sample, which is
why Lecture 2.1 onwards needs no new theory. What it does not give is a
finite-sample guarantee, and a student who thinks it does will over-read a
t-statistic in a sample of twenty.
:::

## Doubling the Sample Size

Suppose we drew 240 people instead of 120, from the same population.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Does the histogram of sample means shift, narrow, do both, or do neither?
:::


::: {.notes}
65-68 min. It narrows and does not shift, and the factor is root two rather
than two, which nearly nobody predicts. The wrong answers are worth more than
the right one: "shifts" means the centre and the spread have not been
separated. Hear the direction before anything is run. Do not
adjudicate.
:::

# Confidence Intervals and Tests

## Building a 95 Per Cent Interval

This section turns an estimate and its standard error into a defensible
statement:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\bar{y} \;\pm\; 1.96 \times \mathrm{se}(\bar{y})
\end{equation}
```

- $1.96$: the 97.5th percentile of the standard normal distribution

::: {.takeaway title="The Interval Runs 11.19 to 13.31"}
$12.25 \pm 1.96 \times 0.54$, and 1.96 is the large-sample value for a skewed
population.
:::

::: {.notes}
IDEA 3, 68-92 min. Say where 1.96 comes from: it is the point beyond which a
standard normal puts 2.5 per cent in each tail. For a genuinely normal
population with sigma estimated we would use the t distribution on 119 degrees
of freedom, whose value is 1.98 and would give 11.18 to 13.32. Above n = 120
the choice makes no practical difference, which is Wooldridge's own remark.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTION 4. Earnings are skewed, so the exact interval of C-5b,
     p.729-730, which assumes a normal population, does not apply. C-5d,
     p.732, equation C.27, licenses y-bar +/- 1.96*se(y-bar) as an
     approximate 95% interval for large n from a nonnormal population, and
     the slide now says "large-sample value". C-6c, p.738: for n > 120 the
     choice between t and standard normal critical values is practically
     irrelevant. ARITHMETIC CHECKED: 12.25 +/- 1.96(0.5395) = 11.19, 13.31;
     the t(119) multiplier 1.98 gives 11.18, 13.32. Numbers come from the
     generator and are unchanged. -->
```

## Coverage Across Repeated Intervals

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{One hundred intervals from one hundred samples; the true mean is a vertical line.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Five in a Hundred Miss"}
Every interval lands somewhere different; the truth at 11.52 stays put. The
rule carries the 95 per cent, not any one interval.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Walk it slowly: one hundred samples of 120, one interval built
from each by the same rule, the truth drawn as a vertical line at 11.52.
Count the marked ones aloud. That count is what the 95 per cent was a promise
about, and it is the only thing it was a promise about. Ask which interval is
ours; the honest answer is that we cannot tell from the data.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- FIGURE 1-3_intervals: 100 horizontal intervals stacked vertically,
     vertical rule at the true mean 11.52, misses in a contrasting colour
     with a heavier stroke. Around five should miss. Do NOT reuse the
     2-4_interval.png geometry - that one shades a density, this one is a
     caterpillar plot.
     Wooldridge C-5a, p.728, table C.2, runs the same demonstration with 20
     replications. -->
```

## Why the 95 Per Cent Describes the Procedure

Throw a ring at a fixed peg. The peg never moves; the throws scatter. The
endpoints jump across the hundred intervals; the truth stays put at 11.52.
Randomness lives in the endpoints, never in the population mean.

::: {.caveat title="Ninety-Five Intervals in a Hundred"}
Before the sample is drawn, the random interval covers $\mu$ with probability
0.95. Once the endpoints are numbers, $\mu$ either sits inside them or does
not.
:::

No sample says whether our own 11.19 to 13.31 covered 11.52.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes, and it is worth being slow. Written out, the correct sentence is
dull and the wrong one is exciting, which is most of why the wrong one wins.
Wooldridge's own wording: probability plays no role once the confidence
interval is computed for the particular data at hand.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-5a, p.727-728. Equation C.17: P(Y-bar - 1.96/sqrt(n) < mu <
     Y-bar + 1.96/sqrt(n)) = .95, a statement about the RANDOM interval
     C.19. p.728: "The probability that mu is in the interval (C.18) is .95.
     This is incorrect... Probability plays no role once the confidence
     interval is computed for the particular data at hand." -->
```

## Wording a Confidence Interval

Only one of these sentences is defensible, and the wrong one sounds better.

::: {.worked title="The Sentence to Avoid"}
"There is a 95 per cent chance the true average lies between 11.19 and 13.31."
:::

::: {.worked title="The Sentence to Use"}
"Our estimate is 12.25 euro, with a 95 per cent confidence interval from 11.19
to 13.31."
:::

The first sentence makes $\mu$ vary; only the endpoints vary [@hoekstra2014robust].

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. A different 120 people would have produced a different pair of
endpoints, and mu would have sat exactly where it sits now. Hoekstra and
co-authors put the wrong sentence to researchers and to students, and both
groups endorsed it. Tell them this is examinable wording, because it is.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-5a, p.728, for both sentences. The two .worked boxes are a
     matched pair, which is the one case the one-callout rule allows. -->
```

## Testing the Mean Against a Claimed Value

Somebody claims average hourly earnings in this population are ten euro. That
claim is the null hypothesis, and the statistic below is the t-statistic:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
t \;=\; \frac{\bar{y} - \mu_0}{\mathrm{se}(\bar{y})}
\end{equation}
```

- $\mu_0$: the null hypothesis, the value the claim asserts, here 10.00
- $t$: how many standard errors $\bar{y}$ sits from $\mu_0$

::: {.takeaway title="t Equals 4.2, Far Into the Tail"}
$(12.25 - 10.00)/0.54 = 4.2$, far into the tail of what the claim would produce.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The statistic measures the distance from the sample mean to the
claimed value in units of the standard error, so it is scale-free. Under the
claim, and with a normal population, it follows a t distribution on n minus one
degrees of freedom; with 119 of those, the normal and the t are practically the
same curve. Angrist and Pischke's rule of thumb is that anything past about two
in absolute value is hard to square with the claim.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-6b, p.735, equation C.35: t = sqrt(n)(y-bar - mu_0)/s =
     (y-bar - mu_0)/se(y-bar), distributed t(n-1) under H0 in a normal
     population. C-6c, p.738, for the nonnormal case at large n. MM appendix
     to ch.1, pp.38-39, for the "bigger than about two" convention.
     ARITHMETIC CHECKED: 2.25/0.5395 = 4.17. -->
```

## What a p-Value Says and What It Does Not

A p-value says what the claim would produce, not whether it is true. It
measures how badly the data embarrasses the claim, not its truth:

- **What a p-Value Is:** The smallest error rate at which the claim would be rejected.
- **Under the Claim:** Fewer than one sample in ten thousand reaches $|t| = 4.2$.

::: {.caveat title="Not the Chance of Error"}
A p-value is not the probability the claim is false. Nor is a p-value the chance
we erred. A large p-value is no evidence the claim is true
[@wasserstein2016asa].
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Wooldridge's definition is the largest significance level at
which we could carry out the test and still fail to reject; the equivalent
reading is the probability of a test statistic at least this extreme when the
claim is true. Both are statements about what the claim would generate, and
neither is a statement about the claim. Note also that we say "fail to reject",
never "accept": many values of mu_0 survive the same sample.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-6d, p.738-739: p-value is the largest significance level at
     which we fail to reject; also "the probability that we observe a value
     of T as large as [t] when the null hypothesis is true". C-6b, p.738, on
     "fail to reject" rather than "accept". ASA statement for the list of
     misreadings.
     CORRECTION 5. The slide read "less than once in a thousand times". The
     two-sided p-value at t = 4.17 on 119 df is 5.8e-05, so "fewer than one
     in ten thousand" is the accurate statement. -->
```

## Significance and the Size of the Gap

A large statistic comes from a large gap or a small standard error:

- **Statistical Significance:** The gap divided by its standard error, which is $t$.
- **Practical Significance:** The size of the gap itself, here 2.25 euro an hour.
- **Why Both Are Reported:** A big sample makes a tiny gap statistically significant.

::: {.takeaway title="Significance Is Not Magnitude"}
Whether 2.25 euro an hour matters is a judgement, not a test result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and it is the frame that keeps Lecture 2.3 honest. Wooldridge's
example is a freeway widening that cuts commuting by 3.6 minutes on a sample of
900: overwhelmingly significant, and a meagre effect. The mechanism is test
consistency - as n grows the test rejects any false null with probability
approaching one, however small the true gap. So report the estimate alongside
the test, always.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-6f, p.742: "an estimate can be statistically significant
     without being especially large in a practical sense"; practical
     significance depends on context and judgement. p.743, test consistency:
     "no matter how close mu is to zero, we can be almost certain to reject
     H0: mu = 0 given a large enough sample size." Example C.9, p.742, is
     the freeway case. -->
```

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

The 95 per cent belongs to the procedure, and the procedure includes sampling.
If the 120 chose themselves, the rule covers less than 95 per cent. The
arithmetic on the slide will not say so.

::: {.notes}
92-97 min. Same slot every week. They answer in pairs first, then you. The
point is not that sampling is hard in the abstract, but that THIS interval
rests on something nameable that may well be false: if the people who answered
are the ones with something to report, every number on the slide is wrong in a
direction the standard error cannot see.
:::

## Application

Simulate the whole exercise, and count:

- **Draw:** 120 people, take the mean, build the interval by the same rule.
- **Repeat:** Five hundred times, recording whether 11.52 falls inside.
- **Change:** The sample size, then see which number shrinks and which holds.

::: {.takeaway title="Coverage Holds, Width Shrinks"}
Raising $n$ narrows every interval and leaves coverage near 95 per cent.
:::

::: {.notes}
97-105 min. Take the prediction before the code runs or the demonstration is
passive: what fraction of the five hundred intervals will contain the truth?
Write the number on the board first. Then run it. The fraction stays put and
the width shrinks, which is the whole lecture in one output. Lab this week:
they write the loop themselves.
:::

## Derivation: Unbiasedness and Consistency of the Sample Mean

Take the expectation of the sample mean. Then take its variance and grow $n$.

::: {.takeaway title="Linearity, Then Independence"}
Linearity of expectation carries part one. Independence of the draws carries
part two, which is what random sampling buys.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

::: {.notes}
Two short parts. For the first, push the expectation through the sum using last
week's rules and use the fact that every drawn person has the same population
mean. For the second, do the same to the variance, notice the n in the
denominator, and say what happens to it as n grows. Wooldridge writes both out:
the unbiasedness algebra is on p.717 and the variance on p.718.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-2b, p.717, for E(Y-bar) = mu. C-2c, p.718, equation C.6,
     for Var(Y-bar) = sigma^2/n. C-3a, p.721-722: an unbiased estimator
     whose variance goes to zero is consistent; the law of large numbers,
     equation C.8, gives consistency even without a finite variance. -->
```

## Derivation: The Standard Error of the Mean

Compute the variance of the sample mean, then take its square root. Replace the
population spread with the sample one.

::: {.takeaway title="Root n Is Not Assumed"}
The root $n$ appears only at the last step, from taking the square root.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

::: {.notes}
Part two of the previous derivation, stopped one step earlier. Reading that
formula and reading the three-panel figure should feel like the same activity.
Flag the last step: sigma is unknown, so s replaces it, which is why the result
is called a standard error rather than a standard deviation. The same shape
reappears in Lecture 2.3 for the slope, with two extra ingredients.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-5b, p.730: se(y-bar) = s/sqrt(n) is the point estimate of
     sd(Y-bar) = sigma/sqrt(n). C-5c, p.733, separates the four quantities:
     sigma, sigma/sqrt(n), s and s/sqrt(n). -->
```
